source.title: Debt Without Chains
source.summary: Sukuk, qard hasan, and reimagining what debt could look like in the 21st century.
source.author: Islamic Economics
source.body_text: What if debt didn't have to be a trap? Qard hasan, the beautiful loan, is lending with no expectation of return beyond the principal, considered one of the most virtuous acts in Islam. Sukuk transform debt into shared ownership of real assets. Diminishing musharakah lets homebuyers gradually purchase their house from the bank as co-owner rather than as debtor. This final episode looks at the alternatives, from microfinance experiments in Bangladesh to sovereign sukuk issued by the UK and Hong Kong, and asks whether Islamic principles can offer a way out of the global debt crisis. With worldwide debt exceeding $300 trillion, the question isn't academic. The 7th-century insight that debt should serve people rather than enslave them may be the most radical financial idea the modern world needs.

threads.post: The Quran permits trade but forbids riba because one creates value while the other extracts it. Trade produces something new. Riba simply moves existing wealth from borrower to lender, compounding forever. Sukuk transform this by turning debt into shared ownership of real assets. Instead of owing money that grows, you own a piece of something tangible. Malaysia has issued sukuk representing $1.7 trillion in assets.
